s42.title: Behind the Bumpers: 111 WildStang and 112 Plus One

s43.title: WildStang and Plus One robot reveal, post 3

bet.text: Pick up from the floor in front and behind with one vertically symmetric gripper, on an arm and lift that can score everywhere with both pieces.

demand.text: Kickoff goals: maximize ranking points and points with five links, scoring high first, then mid, then low, and engage the charge station. Efficiency is called critical to scoring.
A team post says all of the robot's complexity is for six scoring locations.

auto.text: Three pieces from the loading zone side; a second three-piece auto over the cable protector was added before the championship.
Paths are corrected with AprilTags near the grid, and the charge station balance is a simple gyro loop.
It won the Autonomous Award at Seven Rivers.

cycle.text: The operator picks what (piece, height, pickup); the driver picks when. One trigger snaps the robot to the nearest node and extends, another releases.
From the championship, it drives itself to the double substation by AprilTag.
In practice before it: 11 to 12 teleop cycles to the middle links.
A fan's table gives 8.3 teleop pieces per championship qualification match.

endgame.text: Endgame mode stows the arm low and turns the driver's speed trigger into a slowdown for the charge station.
At Midwest, time spent choosing between one more piece and balancing cost it a couple of ranking points.

fallback.text: The driver's stick shifts the automatic alignment for pieces held off center, and an override turns automatic driving off.
Away from tags, auto paths are corrected by odometry.

gave_up.text: Refusing a frame cutout gave up mechanical alignment to the nodes and room for partners to pass behind it while it scored.
The open-top lift is loose at the top; fast strafing with the arm out could pop the carriage out of the lift.
It was too light at about 73 lb and took steel rails as ballast.

changed.text: Before Midwest, sliders replaced carriage side rollers.
After it: a second Limelight, a 100:1 arm reduction with a larger pulley after the arm belt broke, and the wrist encoder moved past the belt.
For the championship: a full rebuild, a protected wrist encoder, and cones fed on their side at the double substation.

outcome.text: 38-5-1 in official play; ranked 32 by championship OPR (67.94, Archimedes).

solves.text: Move fast to cut cycle time while carrying heavy lift and arm loads

cost.text: First arm motion made the chassis jump; the team planned ballast and a slower arm
Module issues were mostly motor keys; all drive motors were replaced before the championship

facts.text: REV MAXSwerve modules; a module with its motor controllers swaps quickly
Outer side rails are solid steel bar, used as ballast against arm and lift loads; expected added weight
The whole robot stayed under 100 lb with it
The driver has 60 percent of speed, and a trigger unlocks the rest
ThriftyBot 3 x 1 in wheels were fitted for Midwest; fitting them meant removing the outer fork
Motors on the robot

functions.name: Open-top lift

solves.text: Let the arm swing from the front to the back of the robot

cost.text: With side roller bearings, a quick strafe or rotation with the arm out could pop the carriage out
Keeping it sturdy was the hardest part and took several iterations

functions.type: continuous cord lift with no top cross member

facts.text: Interlock blocks on the extension stage lock into the fixed stage or the carriage, depending on travel
Constant force springs and magnets keep the moving stage down, well over 50 lb together
Two Igus sliders on each side of the carriage; each takes 157 lb static; some float so they do not bind it
Igus rails guide it and welded steel side stays adjust parallelism
One piece of Spectra per side does up and down, each run
Cord tension aims at twice the lift's stall load, on aluminum-sleeved printed capstans

functions.name: Carbon fiber arm

solves.text: Reach every node and pickup on both sides

cost.text: The arm belt broke in half in the last Midwest practice match; the 18 tooth pulley was outside the maker's load data
Hex inserts and the planetary output rounded out, adding backlash the arm is sensitive to

functions.type: belt-driven single-joint arm on the carriage

facts.text: Carbon fiber tube with printed Onyx end caps and joints
End caps are held with hot glue, so a broken cap comes out with a heat gun and the tube is reused
A destructive test took four to five overhead swings into concrete to break the end caps
After Midwest: NEO, 100:1 planetary, 22 to 28 tooth, 20 mm wide 8 mm pitch Gates belt
Encoder sits after the belt, so a skipped tooth does not lose position

solves.text: Hold the gripper at the precise angle floor pickup needs

cost.text: At Midwest, belt skips changed the encoder offset and disabled arm and gripper
A wrist encoder broke in a Seven Rivers qualification match and the robot was unusable for the rest of it

facts.text: Through-bore encoder gives absolute position without zeroing
After Midwest the encoder moved past the belt; for the championship its axle is supported on both sides

functions.name: Gripper

solves.text: Take cubes, tipped cones and upright cones from either side with one mechanism

cost.text: The intake belt could hop its pulley when hit and disable the gripper at Midwest
A cone was trapped in the front of the robot in a Seven Rivers match; a plastic plate closed that space

functions.type: vertically symmetric roller gripper with polybelt

facts.text: Horizontal rollers act as a top roller for cubes and a pincher for cones; polybelt pushes the cone past the dead zone
The first CAD weighed 11 lb against a 5 lb goal and was cut to just over 6 lb
2 in compliant wheels, 3:1 reduction, 30 A limit while intaking
A constant 10 percent drive holds the piece; cones are ejected at full power, cubes at very low power to limit bounce-out
Low goal: 0.1 s of low power for a cube, then full power for a cone
On first tests it took a cone with the tip toward it within 15 degrees either way
An observer called the manipulator a massive influence on other robots

solves.text: Move lift, arm and wrist together without hitting the robot or the height limit

facts.text: Motions fall into types where arm, lift or wrist waits for another
Each preset stores lift, arm and wrist values for cone and for cube
It waits to extend until the heading is within 15 degrees

solves.text: Keep a tag in sight from every scoring spot instead of trusting odometry

cost.text: With one Limelight and odometry, error grew from about 3 in at the practice field to about 12 in at Midwest, often picking the wrong node
A lighting change at Seven Rivers hid the tags for two matches, which held 5 of the event's 6 drops

facts.text: Two angled Limelights; the one that sees more tags is used, otherwise both are averaged
Drives to the closest cone or cube node for the selected piece
Before the championship the cameras were tilted to see the loading station tag too

functions.name: Piece-request LEDs

solves.text: Tell a human player across the field which piece is wanted

functions.type: LED signal to the human player

facts.text: Yellow for cone, purple for cube, set by the same operator button as the presets

decisions.because: it maximizes electrical space and leaves the end effector free to change over the season
decisions.instead_of: bumper cutouts that align the frame to the grid
decisions.cost: software alignment is needed, the robot sticks out further into the scoring lane, and its two-stage lift may raise the center of gravity

decisions.because: the arm's swing range left no room for cross members at the top of the stage
decisions.cost: it was loose at the top and needed several iterations, with sliders and steel stays, to be sturdy

decisions.because: it works front and back without a twist joint in the wrist
extra mass counteracts the heavy dynamic loads of lift and arm; the team also called about 73 lb too light

decisions.choice: Hot glue for the carbon fiber joints
decisions.because: a broken end cap can be removed and the tube reused
a tag is always in view near the grid

decisions.choice: Tipped cones at the double substation
decisions.because: pickup time there was by far the biggest slowdown, and a cone on its side gives the gripper a much larger target
the team expected close to 12 teleop cycles from it when it threw cubes over the charge station while the others pushed them in
decisions.cost: drive problems put 1561 out in both lost matches
